title: Teachers and AI: Understanding the factors influencing AI integration in K-12 education
extended_summary:
This paper examines the psychological and pedagogical factors that shape K-12 teachers’ readiness to integrate generative AI into instructional practice. The authors focus on why teachers embrace or resist AI, rather than testing an intervention effect with a causal design. The study was motivated by a gap in the literature on how teachers perceive AI’s usefulness, risks, curricular fit, and ethical implications in real classroom settings.

The study was conducted in a private school in Türkiye within an ongoing Digital Learning Academy professional development program. Sixty-six teachers from 11 disciplines participated in a 14-week course on AI in education. Participants engaged with video lessons, online discussion forums, and AI-supported learning activity design tasks using tools such as ChatGPT, MagicSchool, Canva, Gamma, and Character.ai. The data sources were qualitative: forum posts, activity designs, and teachers’ reflections, which were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis.

Findings show that teachers viewed AI as valuable for efficiency, lesson planning, differentiated instruction, personalization, and student engagement. At the same time, they identified barriers including technical problems, heavy workload, curriculum misalignment, language and cultural mismatch, and ethical concerns about privacy, plagiarism, and reduced creativity. The paper concludes that successful AI integration in K-12 education requires not only access to tools but also targeted teacher support, ethical guidance, and better alignment with local curricula and contexts.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a peer-reviewed exploratory qualitative study using thematic analysis of forums and design tasks with 66 K-12 teachers. It is methodologically clear but non-causal and context-specific, so it provides descriptive evidence rather than strong efficacy evidence.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for teacher efficiency and instructional design, but it reports no quantitative impact estimates and no student outcome tests. The likely effect on broader K-12 populations remains unclear because the evidence is perception-based and localized to one private school context.

interventions.use_case: Teacher-facing generative AI tools such as ChatGPT and MagicSchool used in a K-12 professional development setting for lesson planning, content generation, classroom activity design, and instructional support; also includes AI-supported learning activity design tasks and prompt-based content creation.

finding.finding_summary: Teachers consistently reported that generative AI increased efficiency and practicality, especially for creating content quickly, streamlining lesson planning, and supporting data processing/evaluation. The study is qualitative with 66 teachers (n=66) and reports no effect sizes; the evidence is based on thematic analysis of discussion forums and designed activities rather than causal testing.
finding.measure: Qualitative teacher perceptions of efficiency, lesson planning, and workflow support from AI tools

finding.finding_summary: Teachers described students as excited, interested, and more engaged when AI tools were introduced, suggesting a favorable impact on motivation and classroom participation. This is descriptive qualitative evidence from 66 teachers; no effect size or statistical estimate was reported.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported student excitement, interest, and engagement

finding.finding_summary: Teachers believed AI could support critical thinking, collaboration, inquiry, problem solving, and differentiated instruction, but they also worried it could reduce creativity and effort and encourage plagiarism or uncritical copying. Because the paper is exploratory qualitative work with 66 teachers, the findings indicate perceived opportunities and risks rather than causal effects.
finding.measure: Teacher-reported pedagogical affordances and concerns related to critical thinking, collaboration, creativity, and ethical use

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that AI-supported lesson design could enrich instruction across subjects such as mathematics, science, history, literature, and foreign languages through interactive activities, presentations, simulations, and adapted materials. The study is descriptive/interpretive rather than causal, based on 63 activity designs and qualitative analysis of teacher reflections, with no quantitative effect size reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative analysis of AI-supported learning activity designs across subjects
